title: Classification of living organisms; Adaptations interdependence and competition
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for AQA GCSE Biology (8461) (status of the source: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms and clues: 4.7.1-c02 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.7.1-c10 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.7.1-c01 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.7.1-c06 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.6.4-q01, 4.7.1-q01, 4.7.1-q05, 4.7.1-q06, 4.7.1-q08, 4.6.4-q02, 4.7.1-q02, 4.7.1-q07, 4.7.1-q09, 4.6.4-q03, 4.7.1-q03, 4.7.1-q04.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Habitat
items.clue: The place where an organism lives.

items.label: Adaptation
items.clue: A feature that an organism has which enables it to survive in the conditions in which it normally lives.

items.label: Ecosystem
items.clue: The interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment.

items.label: Interdependence
items.clue: Within a community each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc. If one species is removed it can affect the whole community.

questions.stem: A student is given the names of two organisms: Panthera leo and Panthera pardus. Which Linnaean group is given by the shared name Panthera?

options.text: Their order in the Linnaean system
Their family in the Linnaean system
Their genus in the Linnaean system
Their species in the Linnaean system

questions.explanation: Organisms are named by the binomial system of genus and species, so the first part of each name, Panthera, gives the genus that the two organisms share.

questions.stem: Which description matches a community in an ecosystem?

options.text: The populations of every species in a habitat
The individuals of one species in a habitat
The living and non-living parts of a habitat
The non-living conditions found in a habitat

questions.explanation: A community is the populations of all the different species living together in a habitat; the ecosystem is the interaction of that community with the non-living parts of the environment.

questions.stem:
The table shows the mean number of mayfly nymphs collected at four sites along one river.

Site | Dissolved oxygen in mg/dm3 | Mean number of nymphs per sample
W | 9.8 | 42
X | 8.1 | 35
Y | 5.4 | 12
Z | 3.2 | 2

Which conclusion about an abiotic factor is supported by these data?

options.text: Dissolved oxygen is a biotic factor for nymphs
Nymph numbers are constant in the whole river
Other river species are unaffected by low oxygen
Fewer nymphs were found where oxygen was lower

questions.explanation: The data show the mean number of nymphs falling from 42 to 2 as dissolved oxygen falls from 9.8 to 3.2 mg/dm3, so this abiotic factor, oxygen levels for aquatic animals, is linked to the size of the population.

questions.stem:
The table shows the numbers of a predator and of its prey counted in the same community over four years.

Year | Number of prey | Number of predators
1 | 1200 | 30
2 | 900 | 45
3 | 600 | 60
4 | 800 | 40

Which statement is best supported by these data?

options.text: Predators and prey compete for the same food
Numbers stayed constant in a stable community
Other species were unaffected by the change
Prey numbers fell as predator numbers rose

questions.explanation: From year 1 to year 3 the prey fell from 1200 to 600 while the predators rose from 30 to 60, and in year 4 the prey rose as the predators fell, showing how a change in a biotic factor affects the community.

questions.stem: Camels live in hot deserts. Which of these is a behavioural adaptation of a camel to desert conditions?

options.text: It has thick fat stored in a hump on its back
It makes small amounts of concentrated urine
It rests in the shade during the hottest hours
It has long eyelashes that keep out the sand

questions.explanation: Adaptations may be structural, behavioural or functional, and resting in shade is something the camel does, so it is a behavioural adaptation that helps it survive in the conditions in which it normally lives.

questions.stem: Linnaeus classified living things depending on their structure and characteristics. Why were new models of classification later proposed?

options.text: Because much larger numbers of species were discovered
Because improved microscopes showed internal structures
Because fossils of many extinct organisms were discovered
Because bacteria were found in many extreme environments

questions.explanation: As evidence of internal structures became more developed due to improvements in microscopes, and the understanding of biochemical processes progressed, new models of classification were proposed.

questions.stem: A gardener sows seedlings very close together in fertile, well-watered soil in an open bed. Which pair of resources will these plants mainly compete for as they grow?

options.text: Light and mineral ions in the soil
Food and territory around each plant
Mates and shelter from other plants
Food and water taken up from the soil

questions.explanation: Plants in a community or habitat often compete with each other for light and space, and for water and mineral ions from the soil, and crowded seedlings shade each other and draw on the same soil.

questions.stem: Rats reach an island on a ship and begin to eat the eggs of a ground-nesting bird. Which biotic factor does this describe?

options.text: One species outcompeting another species
A new predator arriving in this community
A drop in the moisture levels of the soil
A change in the temperature of this island

questions.explanation: New predators arriving is one of the biotic (living) factors which can affect a community, and the rats are feeding on the birds' eggs.

questions.stem: Bacteria that live in deep sea vents are described as extremophiles. Why?

options.text: They live in water that is warmer than average
They survive by moving away from the hot water
They tolerate the extreme heat for short periods
They live in water of extreme heat and pressure

questions.explanation: Some organisms live in environments that are very extreme, such as at high temperature, pressure, or salt concentration, and these organisms are called extremophiles; bacteria living in deep sea vents are extremophiles.

questions.stem: In the three-domain system developed by Carl Woese, into which three groups are organisms divided?

options.text: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota
Bacteria, Protists and Eukaryota
Archaea, Bacteria and Protists
Archaea, Bacteria and Animals

questions.explanation: Due to evidence available from chemical analysis, organisms are divided into Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota, with protists, fungi, plants and animals included in Eukaryota.

questions.stem: A disease kills nearly all the insects that pollinate several plant species in a woodland. Which outcome best shows interdependence in this community?

options.text: Other woodland species are unaffected by this
Many other species in the wood are affected
Plants are unaffected as they feed themselves
Nothing changes as the community is stable

questions.explanation: This is interdependence: each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc., so if one species is removed it can affect the whole community.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a stable community?

options.text: Population sizes stay exactly the same each year
The species stop competing for food and territory
Species and environmental factors are in balance
The abiotic factors in a habitat stay constant

questions.explanation: A stable community is one where all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain fairly constant.
